prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength brought atomic time and frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep B004 as a single part for Katori and Ye. Seven of eight of us arrive at it from different starting points, and I do not count that as evidence; what persuades me is that no one has produced a scientific objection that survives. The invention is specific: a magic-wavelength lattice makes the trap shift of the clock transition vanish to first order, so that confinement is compatible with an unperturbed transition and thousands of atoms are interrogated in parallel. That is what turned optical clocks from a single-ion accuracy exercise into a stability-and-accuracy regime, and it is the part that was not inherited from 2005 or 2012. The realisation is Ye's: uncertainty near 1e-18, many-body and Fermi-degenerate clock operation, and millimetre-scale redshift measurements, reproduced and compared across NIST, PTB, SYRTE, RIKEN and others for two decades. On the chair's question about the redefinition of the second, my position is that it is neither a condition nor needed as support: the science is complete and the prize is for the invention and its demonstrated performance, not for a later metrological decision. On the distinctness question, the citation should name the magic-wavelength lattice and the neutral-atom ensemble explicitly so that the text itself separates this from the comb and from single-ion control.
statement.case_against: The reservations are real and I do not consider them closed. Optical-clock progress was a race, and Takamoto and Sr-lattice colleagues in Katori's group, and groups at PTB, NIST, SYRTE and RIKEN, made contributions that a two-name credit passes over; I cannot verify the priority record beyond what the shortlist and my own background give. The 2005 and 2012 prizes honoured adjacent ground, and a colleague could reasonably call this a third visit to precision atomic physics. And, as I said in round 1, I am an atomic physicist who values measurement precision; that is a taste, not a neutral criterion, and Danielsson is right to ask whether an instrument and a measurement capability weigh as much as a clue found in nature. I have tried to test my own ranking against that challenge rather than dismiss it, and I still come out with B004, but I state the dependence on this judgement.

responses.point: Danielsson moved from IceCube (B032) to B004 but says he fears choosing the more comfortable attribution over the more consequential discovery, and that B032 may be stronger in a year or two if the NGC 1068 and Galactic-plane picture sharpens.
responses.response: I take this seriously and I would rather have the argument stated than hidden. Where I differ is on what 'consequential' should mean for this year: B032 is a new window on the universe, but the three-name allocation inside a collaboration of hundreds is, by his own account, a judgment he could not verify, and the source-level evidence is still moving. If it firms up, the case becomes stronger next year, which is an argument for patience on B032 and not against awarding a finished result now. I also think the lattice clock is more than an instrument: it gave a new way to measure gravity and tests of constants at a scale not otherwise available, so it does reach nature, though not as a discovery of a new object. I would support revisiting B032 later and I would not want the committee to treat B004 as foreclosing it.

responses.point: Johansson has moved from eighth place to B004, and in his case-against statement refers to Ye being credited under other candidate lines, which the chair has asked to be settled.
responses.response: I welcome the move and I agree with his reasons: the opening placement reflected the pull of one's own field and the worry about overlap, not a flaw in the science. On the factual point, the shortlist file shows Ye only under B004; the other shortlisted parts do not name him, so I read the reference as an error and not as a balance problem. I would ask him to confirm that, since a double credit would matter for the allocation. Separately, since he works in circuit QED, I note that his own caution about B034 following the 2025 prize and the four names for three places is the same sort of argument I would apply there, and it leaves B034 behind B004 in my judgement.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers magic-angle graphene (B010) as a single part for MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Bistritzer, lists B004 as his first alternative, and himself names the age of the field, the unsettled pairing mechanism and contested credit as risks.
responses.response: The Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by the 2018 observation is a real and unusual prediction-then-discovery sequence, and I rank B010 as an alternative for that reason. The difference between us is how much weight an unsettled interpretation deserves. He accepts that the correlated states are established even though the pairing mechanism is not; I would accept that for a field that has had more time, but with eight years of history, continuum-model priority disputes involving Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto, and parallel experimental groups, I think the credit is not yet as clean as the clocks. To his question of what B010 would need to be ready: a clearer mechanism, or a settled history of who first showed what. I would be glad to support it when that arrives, and if he moves to B004 that would not require him to abandon the physics.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the lattice clock is a distinct concept, not the next refinement of the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and raises whether a two-part prize would be fairer than a single part.
responses.response: I agree on distinctness and I want the citation to carry that argument. On a two-part prize, I looked for a pairing that improves the allocation and, like her, have not found one: B023 adds Cirac and Zoller, but I would be adding a theory proposal whose experimental realisations were honoured in 2012, and B016 overlaps with it, so I think a second part would dilute rather than complete the case. I also now rank B023 above B016, which she keeps as her second alternative, because the Cirac-Zoller gate proposal is a sharper and more defined achievement than the Hubbard-simulation claim, where Cirac and Jaksch and others make the credit diffuse.

responses.point: Olsson set aside her first-ranked magic-angle graphene candidate (B010) to support B004, saying she did so on maturity and credit rather than physics.
responses.response: I think that was a principled decision and it is the one I would make too. I want to record that it does not mean B004 won by default: on the grounds she names, the credit for B004 is two names with a clear division of the idea and the performance, and B010 has more open questions. Her willingness to keep B010 as an alternative is the right place for it, and I would keep it there as well.

uncertainties: Whether the citation wording separates the lattice clock from the 2005 comb and 2012 single-ion prizes clearly enough; I propose naming the magic-wavelength lattice and the neutral-atom ensemble explicitly.

Whether Takamoto and other Sr-lattice colleagues, or the PTB, NIST, SYRTE and RIKEN groups, should change the credited names; I cannot verify the priority record from the supplied material and do not think the evidence in the files supports a different set than Katori and Ye.

Whether a committee that weighs discoveries in nature more heavily than measurement capability would judge B032 stronger in a year or two; I think that is a fair prospect and not a reason to hold B004.
I have not verified detailed credit claims against external sources; my judgments rest on the shortlist, the round-1 statements and my own background knowledge.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure in response to the chair's question. My doctoral period included a research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, which is Ye's institution (JILA). My profile documents no personal or collaborative relationship with Katori or Ye, and I have no ongoing tie to JILA; I regard the stay as a historical connection for disclosure and not as a reason to recuse myself or to abstain on B004, but I am content for the committee to weigh it and would accept a different handling if colleagues think it bears on the case. I also have WACQT management links relevant to B034 and European quantum-memory collaborations that could touch B023 and B016, which I would raise if either became a serious contender.
